title: Posterior mediastinum: aorta, azygos vein, and esophagus (anterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: The back walls of the thorax and abdomen: the right posterior intercostal veins, the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, and esophageal, mediastinal, and bronchial veins.
Climbs on the right side of the thoracic vertebral bodies and arches forward over the root of the right lung at about T4.
hy: It joins the systems of the superior and inferior venae cavae, so it can carry blood back to the heart by another route when the inferior vena cava is blocked.

rows: Head, neck, upper limbs, and the wall of the chest. It is formed by the two brachiocephalic veins behind the first right costal cartilage and receives the azygos vein.
hy: Superior vena cava syndrome: obstruction, most often by a lung cancer or lymphoma, causes swelling of the face and arms, a flushed face, and distended neck veins.

rows: Head, neck, and upper limb of its side. It is formed behind the sternoclavicular joint by the internal jugular and subclavian veins.
The left vein is longer and crosses behind the manubrium, in front of the branches of the aortic arch.
The two brachiocephalic veins join to form the superior vena cava.
Head, neck, and upper limb of its side. It is formed behind the sternoclavicular joint by the internal jugular and subclavian veins.
The left vein is longer and crosses behind the manubrium, in front of the branches of the aortic arch.
The two brachiocephalic veins join to form the superior vena cava.
Brain, face, and neck. It begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus.
Descends in the carotid sheath, lateral to the carotid arteries and the vagus nerve.
Joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
hy: The height of its pulsation (jugular venous pressure) reflects right atrial pressure and rises in right heart failure.

rows: Brain, face, and neck. It begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus.
Descends in the carotid sheath, lateral to the carotid arteries and the vagus nerve.
Joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
hy: The height of its pulsation (jugular venous pressure) reflects right atrial pressure and rises in right heart failure.

rows: Upper limb. It continues the axillary vein at the outer border of the first rib.
Crosses the first rib in front of the anterior scalene muscle.
Joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
hy: The thoracic duct empties at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.
A common site for a central venous catheter; the lung apex lies just behind, so a pneumothorax is a risk.

rows: Upper limb. It continues the axillary vein at the outer border of the first rib.
Crosses the first rib in front of the anterior scalene muscle.
Joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
hy: The thoracic duct empties at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.
A common site for a central venous catheter; the lung apex lies just behind, so a pneumothorax is a risk.

rows: Continues the ascending aorta at the level of the sternal angle.
Arches back and to the left over the root of the left lung and becomes the descending aorta at about T4.
Three branches: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian artery.
hy: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum, so an aneurysm of the arch or a mediastinal mass can cause hoarseness.
Coarctation of the aorta usually lies just beyond the origin of the left subclavian artery, near the ligamentum arteriosum.
Baroreceptors in the arch signal through the vagus nerve; those in the carotid sinus signal through the glossopharyngeal nerve.

rows: Continues the aortic arch at about T4.
Descends in the posterior mediastinum, at first on the left of the vertebral column and then in front of it, and passes through the diaphragm at T12.
Chest wall (posterior intercostal arteries), bronchi, esophagus, and pericardium.
hy: In a sudden deceleration injury the aorta tears most often at the isthmus, just beyond the origin of the left subclavian artery.

rows: Aortic arch, as its first and largest branch.
Runs up and to the right and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint.
The right side of the head and neck and the right upper limb, through its two branches, the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.
On the right, the brachiocephalic trunk. On the left, the aortic arch directly.
Ascends in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve and divides at about the upper border of the thyroid cartilage into the internal and external carotid arteries.
Head and neck, through its two end branches. It has no other branches.
hy: At its division lie the carotid sinus, a baroreceptor, and the carotid body, a chemoreceptor; both signal mainly through the glossopharyngeal nerve.

rows: On the right, the brachiocephalic trunk. On the left, the aortic arch directly.
Ascends in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve and divides at about the upper border of the thyroid cartilage into the internal and external carotid arteries.
Head and neck, through its two end branches. It has no other branches.
hy: At its division lie the carotid sinus, a baroreceptor, and the carotid body, a chemoreceptor; both signal mainly through the glossopharyngeal nerve.

rows: On the right, the brachiocephalic trunk. On the left, the aortic arch directly.
Arches over the first rib behind the anterior scalene muscle and becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib.
Upper limb and, through the vertebral, internal thoracic, and thyrocervical branches, the brain, the front of the chest wall, and the neck.
hy: Subclavian steal: a narrowing of the artery before the origin of the vertebral artery reverses flow in that vertebral artery, causing dizziness or fainting when the arm is exercised.

rows: On the right, the brachiocephalic trunk. On the left, the aortic arch directly.
Arches over the first rib behind the anterior scalene muscle and becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib.
Upper limb and, through the vertebral, internal thoracic, and thyrocervical branches, the brain, the front of the chest wall, and the neck.
hy: Subclavian steal: a narrowing of the artery before the origin of the vertebral artery reverses flow in that vertebral artery, causing dizziness or fainting when the arm is exercised.

rows: The lower nine pairs come from the descending thoracic aorta. The first two on each side come from the superior intercostal artery, a branch of the costocervical trunk.
Each runs in the costal groove of its rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles.
The intercostal muscles and overlying skin, the parietal pleura, and, through spinal branches, the vertebrae and spinal cord.
hy: In the costal groove the vein, artery, and nerve lie in that order from above down (VAN), so a needle or chest tube is passed just above the upper border of a rib.

rows: Runs from the pharynx at C6 down through the chest, behind the trachea and the left atrium, and through the diaphragm at T10 to the stomach.
Carries food to the stomach by waves of contraction. Its upper third is striated muscle and its lower third smooth muscle.
hy: Its lower end is a portosystemic anastomosis, where esophageal varices form in portal hypertension.
Long-standing acid reflux changes the lining of its lower end to intestinal-type epithelium (Barrett esophagus), which can turn into adenocarcinoma.

rows: Runs from the cricoid cartilage at C6 to its division into the two main bronchi at the level of the sternal angle. The esophagus lies behind it.
Carries air to and from the lungs. C-shaped rings of cartilage hold it open, and the gap at the back is closed by the trachealis muscle.
hy: In the most common form of tracheoesophageal fistula the upper esophagus ends blindly and the lower esophagus opens into the trachea; the newborn drools, chokes, and turns blue with the first feed.

rows: Runs from the division of the trachea to the hilum of the left lung, passing under the aortic arch and in front of the esophagus.
It is narrower, longer, and more horizontal than the right main bronchus.
